source.title: PopulAtion Parameter Averaging (PAPA)
source.authors: Alexia Jolicoeur-Martineau; Emy Gervais; Kilian Fatras; Yan Zhang; Simon Lacoste-Julien

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments on whether population weight averaging changes held-out accuracy on natural image data, using a different intervention from the listed claim versions. It does not test the specific phenomena in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The reported PAPA, PAPA-all, and PAPA-2 accuracy comparisons are included as results about generalization that fit none of the listed versions. Cited results from other work and results that compare only ensemble performance are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates population parameter averaging, not any of V1–V8. Its own results do not compare random versus natural labels, widths beyond interpolation, convolutional versus fully connected networks, optimizers, batch sizes, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or memorized-example removal. Reporting improved test accuracy alone does not test these versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that population averaging improves single-model generalization, with PAPA generally outperforming its variants and providing larger benefits from scratch than during fine-tuning. They acknowledge greater training cost than a single network and generally better performance from ensembles. Their longer-training comparison has a ResNet-18 exception without augmentation, and PAPA-all performs worse than the baseline in the single-layer logistic-regression experiment.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains populations with weight averaging during training and evaluates test accuracy; it does not use the random-label memorization or generalization-gap measurements in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies by dataset, architecture, training stage, and PAPA variant. The authors report that PAPA tends to outperform PAPA-all and PAPA-2, and that gains are smaller for fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: PAPA average soups have higher reported test accuracy than baseline greedy soups in R1–R8, with smaller gains during fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Population parameter averaging can improve single-model held-out image-classification accuracy over independently trained baseline model soups in the tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: With random augmentations on CIFAR-100, PAPA average soups trained for 300 epochs exceed the mean accuracy of independent models trained for 3000 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Allocating training across a population with parameter averaging can outperform longer independent training in these CIFAR-100 settings.

record.problems: The paper reports accuracy comparisons, not train–test gaps or random-label experiments. Main table comparisons use greedy soups for the baseline and average soups for PAPA; the paper notes baseline greedy soups use one model in the from-scratch settings. Some results are single runs, and uncertainty is not reported for ImageNet.
record.rows_left_out: The main table also reports PAPA-all, PAPA-2, and ensemble accuracies, and the appendices contain detailed sweeps and ablations. These were left out to prioritize the baseline-to-PAPA single-soup comparisons and the longer-training comparison; they do not map to V1–V8.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy comparison.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under controlled tuning.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove a batch-size penalty.
Dropout effects, including training-set size and interactions with augmentation and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, generalization gaps, and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Accuracy after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because none measures a listed effect; this does not dispute the reported accuracy gains. Different architectures, optimizers, and batch sizes used in separate experiments do not constitute controlled tests of V3–V5. Feature similarity and weight-averaging compatibility do not measure V7 sharpness.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and test accuracy; natural-label performance under the specified architectures and training recipes.
Network-width sweep beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under the described tuning conditions.
Large versus small batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and its interaction with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with train–test gaps.
Removing high-influence memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
